title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
hook: a hunter brings Shiva water carried in his mouth and meat he has tasted first

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram: Sambandar, the boy fed by the Goddess, singing of the thief who stole his heart. When a sharp question came, did you answer with what you'd seen? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

Water, carried up a hill in a man's mouth, because he has no pot. Wildflowers, tucked into his hair, because his hands are full. A piece of roasted meat, which he has bitten into first, to make sure it's tender and good. A young hunter climbs into a forest shrine and lays all of this before Shiva. He spits the water over the stone to wash it. He shakes the flowers from his hair. He sets down the meat. Then he stands guard all night with his bow. Today, the hunter the Tamil Shaiva saints call Kannappa.
screen: `WATER CARRIED IN HIS MOUTH.` → `FLOWERS IN HIS HAIR.` → `MEAT HE TASTED FIRST.`

segments.voice: His story is told in the Periya Puranam, in paraphrase. The shrine already has a priest, a careful man who comes each morning with pure water and proper flowers. And each morning he finds the place littered with bones and wilted blossoms, and he grieves, and cleans it all, and worships again. At last Shiva tells him: hide tomorrow, and watch. So the priest hides. The hunter arrives, and sees something terrible. Blood is running from one eye of Shiva's image. He tries herbs from the forest. Nothing stops it. So he takes an arrow, cuts out his own eye, and presses it to the place. The bleeding stops. He laughs with joy. Then the other eye of the image begins to bleed. He knows what to do now, but once his second eye is gone he won't be able to find the spot. So he sets his foot on it, to mark the place, and raises the arrow to his own face. And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and holds his hand. Stop, Kannappa, Shiva says, and the story has him say it again. Turn it once. Notice what the story doesn't do. It doesn't mock the priest. His worship was right, and Shiva honors it by letting him see. It shows him a second kind of love, one that knew none of the rules and held nothing back. Turn it again. The foot on the sacred image, the meat, the water from a mouth. By the rules, each one is wrong. And the story keeps every one of them in. Sundarar, in a hymn listing the Lord's servants, names Kannappa among them. Even a saint who knew every rule counted the hunter as one of his own.
screen: `A PRIEST WHO GRIEVES EACH MORNING` · `THE IMAGE BEGINS TO BLEED` · `A FOOT TO MARK THE PLACE` · `STOP, KANNAPPA`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the offering you actually have. Sit, and let the breath slow. Think of something you'd like to give today: to someone you love, to your work, to God if you pray. Notice the ideal version, the one you'd give if you had more time or more skill. Set it aside. Now look at what's really in your hands this morning. A tired hour. A short call. A clumsy word of thanks. Hold that, just as it is, and let it be enough to give. If you pray, you can offer it the way the hunter did, without polishing it first. The bell holds the time.
Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Today, Kannappa, the hunter who knew none of the rules, gave his eye to stop Shiva's image bleeding, and was stopped by Shiva's own hand. Today's word.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Today, give one thing as it is, a rough note, a short visit, a plain meal, instead of waiting until it's perfect. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Kannappa is honored among the Nayanmars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country, and his story is told at the Shiva temple of Kalahasti, the hill shrine where tradition places it.

what a scholar hears: Sundarar's Tiruttondattokai, the hymn listing the Lord's servants, names Kannappa, and the Periya Puranam tells the life of each saint it lists.

notes: Editor pass: the writer's draft retold the recovery of the Tevaram from the sealed room at Chidambaram, already told on day 1370. Rewritten as a new angle on the same index line: Kannappa, one of the Nayanmars, with a link to Sundarar's Tiruttondattokai. New practice and carry.
